source.title: Generalization Below the Edge of Stability: The Role of Data Geometry
source.authors: Tong-Tong Liang; Alexander Cloninger; Rahul Parhi; Yu-Xiang Wang

record.tranche_reason: The paper tests how data geometry affects learning noisy labels and the timing of memorization using two-layer ReLU experiments; it does not reproduce the original fully random-label setup.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Zhang et al. (2017) and Arpit et al. (2017), but those cited results are not rows. Its own experiments train on labels formed from a teacher function plus Gaussian noise. It reports noisy-label fitting and clean-MSE trajectories, not results for completely random labels, shuffled pixels, or a sweep over corruption fractions.
record.test_reason: The study's noisy-teacher regression trajectories bear on V6: MNIST inputs show initial learning of the teacher signal followed by later noise fitting. It does not directly test completely random classification labels.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors argue that data geometry governs stability-induced implicit regularization: geometries resistant to shattering favor shared representations, while easily shattered geometries favor memorization. Their experiments illustrate geometry-dependent noise fitting; their theory characterizes BEoS solution classes rather than proving the temporal order of learning.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes below-edge-of-stability generalization, mainly theoretically for two-layer ReLU networks, and runs synthetic noisy-teacher experiments; it does not use the original random-label intervention or deep-network settings.
record.method_sensitivity: Input geometry changes the observed rate and extent of noisy-label memorization: Gaussian and spherical inputs fit noise rapidly, while MNIST and a low-dimensional mixture resist overfitting longer.

fits_no_version.finding: Gaussian inputs rapidly reach noisy-label interpolation, whereas MNIST inputs resist interpolation much longer under the same training recipe.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Input geometry affects the speed of memorizing additive label noise.

fits_no_version.finding: Sphere inputs yield final clean MSE 1.0249, near noise variance 1; a union of 20 lines yields 0.07 under the same training recipe.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Input geometry affects the extent of additive-noise fitting within a fixed training budget.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 3.6 constructs width-at-most-n ReLU networks interpolating arbitrary bounded labels on distinct spherical inputs with bounded Hessian norm.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Arbitrary-label interpolation on spherical inputs can coexist with low curvature; this existence result does not establish that gradient training finds it.

record.problems: The experiments use noisy teacher labels rather than fully random labels. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the cited comparisons. The MNIST and Gaussian trajectories are qualitative in the supplied text; Figure 8 is not accompanied by exact values.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for Figure 3 or Figure 4: Figure 3 reports clean-MSE scaling experiments across radial parameters and intrinsic dimensions, and Figure 4 reports activation statistics, but neither measures the V6 timing of learning shared patterns versus memorizing noisy labels.

untested.parts: Training standard deep networks on completely random labels, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Training-time ratios for true versus random labels and convergence across corruption fractions.
The same deep networks fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs under the original fitting setup.
A corruption-fraction sweep with perfect training fit and test error approaching chance.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and augmentation on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.

Natural classification labels versus fully random labels, and whether signal precedes noise fitting on Gaussian inputs. The demonstrated ordering uses a synthetic teacher on MNIST inputs and a two-layer ReLU network.

record.verdict_notes: Fast noise fitting alone neither challenges nor limits V6. The clean-MSE measurements compare predictions with noiseless teacher outputs at training inputs and should not be described as held-out test error.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random labeling, chance test error, and whether fitting it requires unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Training-time comparison against true labels and convergence as the corrupted-label fraction varies.
Fitting shuffled, permuted, or Gaussian-noise inputs with random labels.
A sweep from clean to fully random labels and the corresponding training and test error trajectory.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and augmentation on random-label fitting or true-label generalization.

The experiments use teacher labels with additive Gaussian noise, not fully random labels; the reported MNIST and Gaussian comparison does not directly compare learning trajectories on true versus fully random labels.

rows.subject: two-layer ReLU network
rows.operation_detail: Trained on teacher-function outputs plus Gaussian noise; tracked training loss and clean MSE.

conditions.value: fixed two-layer ReLU teacher plus ξi ∼ N (0, 1)

rows.measure: Training-loss and clean-MSE trajectory; whether noise memorization followed initial learning of the teacher pattern.
rows.value: MNIST inputs initially decrease both training loss and clean MSE; interpolation is resisted for thousands of epochs, and clean MSE starts to increase only after thousands of epochs.
rows.note: The text describes the temporal pattern, but gives no exact trajectory values in the prose. Labels are noisy teacher outputs, not random labels.
rows.check: The reported trajectory supports signal learning before later noise fitting. Clean MSE is evaluated against the teacher on training inputs, not held-out test data. The precise temporal description appears in Appendix C.2.

conditions.value: Gaussian inputs xi ∼ N (0, Id ), d = 784, n = 30000
fixed two-layer ReLU teacher plus ξi ∼ N (0, 1)

rows.measure: Training-loss and clean-MSE trajectory; timing of noisy-label interpolation.
rows.baseline: MNIST inputs under the same architecture, initialization, learning rate, and gradient clip threshold
rows.value: On Gaussian inputs, training loss vanishes and clean MSE rises to the noise limit within a few hundred steps.
rows.note: Comparator condition. The Gaussian-input result shows rapid noise interpolation, but does not report fully random labels or whether real patterns are learned first.
rows.check: Rapid interpolation within a few hundred steps does not establish whether teacher signal precedes noise fitting. V6 specifies an order, not a minimum delay; this result therefore does not justify the extracted limits_scope verdict.

rows.subject: two-layer ReLU network
rows.operation_detail: Trained on noisy labels generated from a fixed quadratic teacher; evaluated final true MSE against the noiseless teacher.
rows.measure: Final true MSE against the noiseless teacher; comparison with noise variance.
rows.note: The sphere condition fits noisy labels to approximately the noise limit, but the reported final metric does not establish that shared patterns were learned first.
rows.check: Final clean MSE of 1.0249 measures noise fitting, not the order of learning signal and noise. It cannot establish partial V6. Figure 6 separately reports interpolation before epoch 2000.

rows.subject: two-layer ReLU network
rows.operation_detail: Trained on noisy labels generated from a fixed quadratic teacher; evaluated final true MSE against the noiseless teacher.

conditions.value: union of 20 randomly oriented 1-dimensional subspaces in R50

rows.measure: Final true MSE against the noiseless teacher; comparison with zero error.
rows.note: The low final clean MSE indicates resistance to overfitting noisy labels in this condition; it does not directly establish the temporal claim in V6.
rows.check: Final clean MSE of 0.07 measures resistance to noise fitting, not the temporal ordering required by V6. It cannot establish partial V6.

relationships.condition: MNIST inputs with synthetic teacher outputs plus additive Gaussian noise
relationships.reason: R1 reports that training loss and clean MSE initially decrease, while clean MSE increases only after thousands of epochs, consistent with learning shared signal before memorizing noise.
relationships.display_finding: Training loss and clean mean squared error initially decreased, with clean error increasing only after thousands of epochs.

reader_labels.condition: MNIST inputs with teacher labels plus additive Gaussian noise
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports that both training loss and clean MSE initially decrease, with clean MSE increasing only after thousands of epochs (R1). This supports learning the teacher pattern before later noise memorization in this setting.
